passage: Raghav, ten, helped at his uncle's roadside dhaba till the last trucks pulled away, then slept on a cot beside the clattering kitchen. At the village school next morning, Masterji said, "Copy the sums from page forty, then underline the answers." Raghav copied the sums and forgot the rest. His head drooped onto his slate. "Lazy again?" Masterji asked. Raghav's eyes stung. "I'm trying, sir." His friend Kunal whispered, "You look like a ghost." At lunch Kunal let him lie in the shade of the neem tree while he kept watch, and shook him awake at the bell. That afternoon Raghav got every sum right.

qa.q: Which page did Masterji ask the class to copy sums from?
qa.a: Page forty.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when Masterji called him lazy?
qa.a: He felt hurt and ashamed; his eyes stung because he really was trying, just too tired to keep up.

qa.q: How could Masterji support Raghav better?
qa.a: He could gently ask how Raghav is sleeping instead of calling him lazy, and talk with the family about the late nights at the dhaba.

qa.q: How does Kunal see what is happening to Raghav?
qa.a: Kunal sees a friend who is worn out rather than lazy, so he lets Raghav nap in the shade and wakes him at the bell.

grounding: Shows a sleep-deprived schoolchild forgetting instructions, getting teary and being called lazy when the real problem is a foggy, tired mind.

passage: Tariq, nine, slept on the other side of a thin wall from his new baby sister, and she cried most nights. At school in Toronto he forgot his library book, then forgot the art instructions twice. When his partner Bao took the blue paint first, Tariq shouted, "You always do that!" and then, to his own surprise, began to cry. The teacher, Ms Harper, crouched by his desk. "You look really tired. How's sleep at home?" Tariq told her about the baby. She sent a note home, and that evening his parents moved his bed into the quieter study.

qa.q: What did Bao take first?
qa.a: The blue paint.

qa.q: Why did Tariq shout at Bao and then cry?
qa.a: He was exhausted, so a small thing felt huge; then he felt surprised and overwhelmed by his own outburst.

qa.q: Which step made a real difference, and why?
qa.a: Ms Harper asking about sleep instead of scolding; it led to a note home and a quieter room, which tackled the cause rather than the behaviour.

qa.q: What might the moment have been like for Bao?
qa.a: Bao may have felt confused or hurt at being shouted at over paint, without knowing how tired Tariq was.

grounding: Illustrates a tired child forgetting instructions and becoming argumentative and teary, and an adult looking for the sleep problem behind it.

passage:
"Bhavna, page forty-two. Ma'am said forty-two."
"Thanks, Kamal."
"I forgot. Again."
"You look like a zombie."
"The sangeet next door went on till one. Then the dhol till three."
"And the test is now?"
"Now. I read the first question four times and it keeps sliding off."
"Bhavna, careless again?"
"Sorry, Ma'am."
"Ma'am, she's not being careless. She couldn't sleep, there was a wedding next door."
"Is that true, Bhavna?"
"Yes, Ma'am. I'm trying. My head is all foggy." Her eyes filled.
"All right. Drink some water, do what you can, and you can finish the rest tomorrow after a proper sleep."

qa.q: Till what time did the dhol play next door?
qa.a: Till three.

qa.q: How was Bhavna feeling during the test?
qa.a: She felt foggy and frustrated, close to tears, because the question kept sliding off however hard she tried.

qa.q: How did Kamal help Bhavna?
qa.a: Kamal explained the lost sleep to Ma'am, so the teacher saw a tired child instead of a careless one.

qa.q: What changed for Ma'am once she heard about the wedding?
qa.a: She stopped calling Bhavna careless and offered water and time to finish after a proper sleep.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild with too little sleep forgetting instructions and turning teary, labelled careless until the tiredness is understood.

passage: Last month, when my baby sister was new, I hardly slept. She cried at night and I lay awake counting cracks in the ceiling. At school I forgot my maths book three days in a row, and Sir wrote "careless" in my diary. At football I shouted at Uday for one bad pass, and then I cried in the toilets, which I never do. Uday found me there. "Mohit, you're not angry, you're sleepy," he said. That night Mamma let me sleep in Dadi's room, far from the crying. The next day I remembered my book.

qa.q: What did Sir write in the diary?
qa.a: Sir wrote "careless" in the diary.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling in the toilets after football?
qa.a: Mohit felt upset and ashamed, crying after shouting at Uday, because tiredness had made everything too much.

qa.q: What finally helped Mohit remember the book?
qa.a: Sleeping in Dadi's room, far from the crying, so Mohit got real rest instead of just trying harder.

qa.q: How does Uday see Mohit's shouting?
qa.a: Uday sees past the anger to the tiredness and says so kindly instead of staying offended.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild short of sleep forgetting things, snapping and crying, being labelled careless, and recovering once real rest is possible.

passage:
Coach's notes, Wednesday
Nitin dropped two easy catches today and twice forgot where I'd placed him. When I called him over, he argued, then his eyes filled up. Last month he was my sharpest fielder, so I didn't send him to run laps. I asked about his evenings. Tuition till eight, homework till eleven, then his cousin's phone games till past midnight. He said, "I try, Coach, but my head is like fog."
I let him sit out the last drill with water and a banana. I called his father tonight and told him what Nitin said. His father was surprised and said they would move the phone out of the room at night.
Harsha

qa.q: Until what time did Nitin do homework?
qa.a: Homework till eleven.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his eyes filled up?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and ashamed, trying hard but unable to focus through the fog in his head.

qa.q: Why was asking about evenings wiser than sending Nitin to run laps?
qa.a: It uncovered the real cause, too little sleep, which laps could not fix, and led to a call home and a change at night.

qa.q: How might Nitin's father feel on getting the call?
qa.a: Surprised and probably concerned, but ready to act by moving the phone out of the room.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild short of sleep becoming foggy, forgetful and argumentative, and a coach looking for the cause instead of punishing effort.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Worst day. Last night the neighbours had a wedding band till late and I couldn't sleep. Today in class my eyes kept closing. Ma'am told us to do questions 1 to 5 on page 42, and I did 6 to 10. Varun laughed. I told him to shut up and then I started crying, in front of everyone! Ma'am said I was being careless. I wasn't. My head felt like cotton wool and I was trying SO hard.
At home Mummy saw my face and asked what happened. When I told her about the band, she said, 'You're not lazy, you're tired.' She wrote a note to Ma'am. Early bed tonight.
Mehak

qa.q: Which questions did Mehak do by mistake?
qa.a: Mehak did questions 6 to 10.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when Ma'am called the work careless?
qa.a: Mehak felt hurt and misunderstood, having tried hard with a foggy, sleepy head.

qa.q: How could Ma'am support a child like Mehak next time?
qa.a: Ma'am could gently ask whether Mehak had slept well, instead of calling the mistake careless.

qa.q: What might Mummy's note help Ma'am understand?
qa.a: It could show Ma'am that the mistakes came from a sleepless night, not laziness, so she can respond kindly.

grounding: A schoolchild short of sleep forgets instructions, turns teary and is called careless, though effort alone cannot fix the fog.
